title: Building on Others in Discussions
keyIdea: A good discussion grows. Instead of repeating what someone said, you build on it: keep their idea and add something new, such as a reason, an example or a fact. Ask follow-up questions about what the speaker actually said, keep questions specific, and if the talk drifts, ask a question that links back to the main topic.

kid: In a class discussion, everyone works on one question together. Your job is not just to say your own idea. It is to help the whole talk move forward.

The best way is to build on what someone said. Keep their idea and add something new. If Ava says a longer lunch gives more time to play, you could say, "Yes, and running around might help us focus in the afternoon." Saying "I agree, more time to play" only repeats her.

You can also build with a follow-up question. Start from the speaker's exact words: "Why do you think they run out of time?" Make it specific. "What about stuff?" is too vague for anyone to answer. A fact or example makes a remark stronger, so back your ideas up.
Talk often drifts, one remark at a time, until nobody is on the question. You can steer it back kindly. Say something like, "That's interesting, but how does it help us decide about lunch?"
adult: This speaking and listening skill (ages 10 to 11, Common Core SL.5.1c) asks learners to pose and respond to specific questions and to make comments that contribute to a discussion and elaborate on the remarks of others. It is the step from taking turns to talking with each other, which researchers call exploratory or dialogic talk.

Elaborating means linking to a previous remark and adding to it: a reason, an example, evidence, a consequence or a respectful challenge. Useful sentence starters are "Building on what Leo said...", "Can you say more about...?" and "I see it differently because...". Follow-up questions that start from the speaker's words are the clearest sign that a learner was really listening.

Common mistakes: repeating a classmate's point in new words and calling it agreement; going off topic with a personal story; asking vague questions such as "What about it?"; giving opinions with no reason ("because I want to"); following a drift instead of steering back; and commenting on the person rather than the idea.

In the lab learners choose a reply that builds rather than repeats, ask two follow-up questions, link facts to the remarks they support, steer a drifting discussion back with a linking question, and sort vague and specific questions. At home, try the "yes, and" game at dinner: each person must add something new to the last idea.

familyTip: At dinner, pick a question like "Should kids get pocket money?" Take turns, but each person must start with "Building on what you said..." and add a reason, example or follow-up question. If the talk drifts, anyone can ask a question that brings it back.

practice.prompt: Zoe says, "Our class should have a reading corner." Which reply builds on her idea?
choices: Yes, and a comfy corner might get more of us reading at break.
Yes, our class should have a reading corner.
I read a comic last night.
practice.hint: Which reply keeps Zoe's idea and adds something new?
practice.explain: The first reply keeps the reading corner idea and adds a new reason. The second only repeats it, and the third is off topic.

practice.prompt: Omar says, "{n} people in our class walk to school." Which follow-up question builds on what he said?
choices: Would more people walk if there were a safe crossing?
What is your favourite colour?
What about stuff?
practice.hint: A follow-up starts from the speaker's own words.
practice.explain: The crossing question starts from Omar's point about walking and pushes it further. The others are off topic or too vague.

practice.prompt: Which question is the most specific?
choices: How many minutes does the walk to school take?
What about the walk?
Is walking good or whatever?
practice.hint: Which one could someone answer clearly?
practice.explain: A specific question names exactly what you want to know, here the number of minutes.

practice.prompt: Lily says, "Recycling helps." Tom adds, "Our school recycled {n} bags of paper last month." What did Tom add?
choices: Evidence that backs up Lily's remark
A repeat of Lily's idea
An off-topic story
practice.hint: Is Tom's remark an opinion or a fact?
practice.explain: Tom gives a fact, the number of bags, which backs up Lily's remark. That is building with evidence.

practice.prompt: A talk about the school garden drifts onto a TV show. What should you say?
choices: That sounds fun, but what should we grow in the garden?
Which episode was the best?
Stop talking, this is boring.
practice.hint: Which reply links back to the main question?
practice.explain: Being friendly and then asking a linking question steers the talk back without upsetting anyone.

pool.prompt: What does it mean to build on someone's remark?
choices: Keep their idea and add something new
Say their idea again in different words
Change the subject to your own idea
pool.hint: Think about what makes a discussion move forward.
pool.explain: Building on a remark means linking to it and adding a reason, example, fact or question.

pool.prompt: Kai says, "We should have {n} minutes of quiet reading each day." Which reply builds on it?
choices: Yes, and quiet reading could help us calm down after lunch.
Yes, quiet reading every day.
Kai always wants to read.
pool.hint: One reply adds a new reason. One repeats. One is about the person.
pool.explain: The first reply adds a new reason. Repeating adds nothing, and talking about Kai instead of the idea is not fair.

pool.prompt: Ella says, "The library is always too noisy." Which follow-up question is best?
choices: When is it the noisiest?
Do you like books?
What about the library and stuff?
pool.hint: Which question digs into Ella's exact point about noise?
pool.explain: Asking when it is noisiest builds on her point and could help solve it. The others are general or vague.

pool.prompt: Max says, "Phones should be allowed at school because I want mine." What is missing?
choices: A real reason or example
A longer sentence
A question for Max
pool.hint: Is wanting something a strong reason?
pool.explain: Wanting something is not evidence. Max needs a reason or example, such as using a phone to check the bus time.

pool.prompt: A discussion about the class trip has drifted to pets. Which question steers it back?
choices: Fun! So which place would we learn most from?
How many pets do you have?
Can we be quiet now?
pool.hint: Look for a kind question that links to the main topic.
pool.explain: A friendly linking question brings the talk back to the trip. The others follow the drift or shut people down.

pool.prompt: Which question is too vague to answer well?
choices: What about things?
How long is the trip?
Why do you think the bus is late?
pool.hint: Which one does not say what it wants to know?
pool.explain: "What about things?" does not name anything, so nobody can answer it clearly.

pool.prompt: Noah says, "Sports day should be in June." Ivy adds, "Last year it rained {n} times in May but only once in June." What has Ivy done?
choices: Backed up Noah's idea with evidence
Repeated Noah's idea
Changed the subject
pool.hint: Is the rain remark a new fact about Noah's idea?
pool.explain: Ivy adds a fact that supports Noah's idea, so she builds on it with evidence.

pool.prompt: Why are follow-up questions useful in a discussion?
choices: They show you listened and help the speaker explain more
They let you change the subject
They make the talk end sooner
pool.hint: What happens when you ask about what someone just said?
pool.explain: A follow-up question starts from what someone said, so it shows you listened and helps them say more.

pool.prompt: Grace says, "We need more benches in the playground." Which reply is about the idea, not the person?
choices: Yes, the old benches are always full at lunch.
Grace just wants to sit down.
Grace always complains.
pool.hint: Talk about the idea, not the speaker.
pool.explain: Good replies respond to the idea. Comments about Grace herself do not help the discussion.

visual.caption: Ava says, "A longer lunch would give us more time to play." Which replies build on her idea? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: Yes, and play helps us focus later.
Why do you think play helps?
Last week we had no time to play.
I agree, more time to play.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: build on a reply, ask follow-up questions, back remarks with evidence, steer drifting talk back on track and sharpen vague questions.
